Don't blame Intel's (INTC) weak guidance, tied to a prolonged memory chip supply shortage, for the fresh rout on tech stocks.
Blame the hyperscalers like Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL) and Meta (META) for not guiding Wall Street properly on how much they intended to spend this year and next on AI infrastructure. The bills are coming in much larger than expected, and Wall Street can't stomach it.
That's why you aren't seeing many heroes out there saying buy the dip right now. That's why Friday is shaping up to be another bloodbath for tech stocks.
Remember, it's cash flow that will be used to repay all the debt hyperscalers are poised to incur to support their robust AI infrastructure buildouts. The fact that cash flow is drying up because of a protracted period of spending is the bug causing the debt and stock markets to catch a cold.
Kudos to Amazon for at least not burying its free cash flow metric, the most important metric for tech at the moment, at the bottom of its earnings release. It made it no less tough to stomach, but at least it was easy to find quickly.
Amazon's free cash flow decreased to an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months, driven primarily by a year-over-year increase of $94.8 billion in purchases of property and equipment. This increase primarily reflects investments in artificial intelligence, Amazon said.
This compares to a free cash flow inflow of $14.8 billion for the trailing twelve months ended Sept. 30 of last year.
"We still expect 2026 cash capex of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027," Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on his earnings call.
Amazon's stock is down 7% in pre-market trading today.
On Wednesday evening, Google posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the quarter versus a Wall Street estimate for negative $3.5 billion.
Thursday saw more than $500 billion in market value wiped off Google.
Meta dropped a bombshell in its third quarter results last week, posting negative free cash flow for the first time since 2012. SpaceX (SPCX) burned about $9.9 billion in free cash flow in the quarter.
Both stocks have continued to sell off post earnings.
Hyperscaler free cash flow is likely to stay negative points out EvercoreISI strategist Julian Emanuel. The hyperscaler cohort of Meta, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Oracle (ORCL) and SpaceX (SPCX) is now near a negative $200 billion expected over the next year Emanuel's research shows.
This is what the market is pricing in today. Painful, yes.

A $2.2 billion underwriting loss in 2025 certainly isn’t anything to celebrate, but when it comes to U.S. commercial auto insurers, there may be a reason to crack a smile.
According to a new report from AM Best, the loss was a 55% improvement compared with the prior year. Any improvement is welcomed for a line that has performed worse than any other commercial insurance line of business over the last decade. Net premiums written increases 6% year-over-year, and incurred losses were basically flat.
Together, U.S. commercial auto insurers have booked a loss in underwriting each year since 2015. Some of its best years during this time were during the COVID pandemic because fewer vehicles were on the road.
Commercial auto’s adverse reserve development in 2025 fell to its lowest level of the last 10 years, and there be some momentum as the direct loss ratio for commercial auto was 66.1 for the first half of 2026. The combined ratio improved to 96.6 in 2025 from 101.4 the prior year.
The physical damage component of losses in commercial auto recorded a $2.4 billion gain, as insureds “that have been more proactive with fleet monitoring and maintenance have benefited from a reduction in the frequency of preventable accidents, which has likely aided overall auto physical damage profitability,” explained David Blades, associate director of industry research at AM Best.
Not everything is looking up. On the liability side, the segment’s underwriting loss in 2025 was more than $4.6 billion – not good, but better than losses of $6.39 in 2024 and $5.9 in 2023. Still, liability accounts for 77% of commercial auto’s NPW, so it affects profit the most. Liability is impacted by adverse social and economic inflation trends on claims costs.
For buyers, improved financial results in commercial auto have brought some pricing relief. AM Best said increases during the second quarter 2026 were the lowest in more than 10 years.

A federal judge on Thursday struck down the Trump administration’s new guidance on who can qualify for a “medically frail” exception to new Medicaid work requirements. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)
Medicaid recipients who are disabled or have a chronic illness will not have to prove they are unable to work to be exempted from new work requirements that take effect next year, a federal judge ruled Thursday.
The decision by U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston grants a partial victory to the 25 Democratic-led states that sued the Trump administration in June, arguing that its new “medically frail” designation was too narrow and would make it too difficult for ill and disabled people to remain on Medicaid, the joint federal-state health insurance program for people with low incomes.
However, the decision also granted some concessions to the administration, most notably by allowing the new work requirements included in the measure known as the One Big Beautiful Big Act to remain in place.
Under that broad 2025 tax and spending law, states that have expanded Medicaid to cover more adults under the Affordable Care Act must require enrollees to work, go to school or volunteer for at least 80 hours a month.
In addition to the 40 states (plus the District of Columbia) that have expanded Medicaid under the ACA, the new rules will apply to Georgia, Tennessee and Wisconsin, which have used federal waivers to expand their Medicaid programs.
In June, the Trump administration released interim guidelines stating that in order to qualify for a “medically frail” exception to the work rules, a Medicaid recipient had to have a significant condition and be significantly impaired in their ability to work.
In a statement unveiling the new guidance, Dr. Mehmet Oz, director of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said it would help Medicaid enrollees “build skills and independence through work, education, job training, or community service, creating new opportunities for themselves and their families.”
Stateline reached out to CMS, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and the White House for comment on Thursday’s ruling but did not receive a response in time for publication.
Before the new guidance, states had been operating under the assumption that they would use the federal government’s traditional “medically frail” designation, which includes five distinct categories of disabilities and illnesses but does not require Medicaid agencies to determine whether the person can work.

Final pitch over Missouri abortion ban turns to fight over voter power
As Election Day approaches, supporters and opponents of Amendment 3 are linking the abortion debate to broader battles over political influence, redistricting and the power of voters

As Missouri voters prepare to decide whether to reinstate the state’s abortion ban, the final arguments over Amendment 3 are reaching beyond abortion itself.
The campaigns are linking the measure to other questions on Tuesday’s ballot and framing the election as a fight over who holds power in Missouri — voters, politicians or wealthy outside interests.
To supporters of Amendment 3, which aims to repeal the state’s 2024 reproductive rights amendment, the threat comes from wealthy out-of-state liberals trying to turn Missouri into a haven for abortion.
“No on 6. Tell billionaires keep their paws off our laws,” read signs at a Yes on 3 rally Tuesday in Arnold.
To opponents of Amendment 3 who are aiming to keep abortion legal, the threat comes from Republican politicians trying to overturn the will of Missouri voters.
“Vote No on 3. Vote No on A. Voters decide. Not politicians,” read signs at a Stop the Ban rally Saturday in St. Louis.
Proposition A is a referendum on a gerrymandered congressional map drawn last year by Republicans. Amendment 6 would require support from at least 80% of both legislative chambers for lawmakers to put a change to a voter-approved initiative back on the ballot.
Both measures appear on the Nov. 3 ballot alongside Amendment 3.
If Amendment 3 fails and Amendment 6 passes, it would be nearly impossible for the Republican-led statehouse to put another measure with abortion restrictions before voters.
Amber Jones, program manager with the nonprofit LeadMO, said tying Proposition A to Amendment 3 is about protecting the people’s power. It’s a message she said resonated with voters as she helped collect signatures from Missourians across the state to put the gerrymandered map on the ballot.
“A handful of powerful people shouldn’t be able to rig the rules to protect themselves,” Jones said. “That is what this fight is about. They want to divide communities, manipulate who gets represented together and make it harder for voters to hold politicians accountable.”
More than 600 volunteers with abortion-rights groups, labor unions and voter advocacy groups knocked on 14,000 doors across the state Saturday, urging voters to oppose Proposition A and Amendment 3, according to a press release from Abortion Action Missouri.

Judge rejects constitutional challenge to Missouri property tax caps tied to stadium bill
Cole County judge rules taxpayers, school districts and counties lack standing to sue, rejecting claims that the law unfairly treats different counties
Cole County Circuit Judge Christopher Limbaugh ruled that property tax caps included in a bill to support professional sports stadiums are constitutional(Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
A Cole County judge on Wednesday rejected a constitutional challenge to property tax caps lawmakers added to a bill aimed at keeping the Kansas City Chiefs in Missouri.
The caps, structured as credits against property tax bills, applied to 97 of Missouri’s 114 counties. The caps, voted on in April, will mean this year’s property tax bill cannot be higher than last year in up to 22 counties, and cannot increase more than 5% in 75 others.
Of the 97 counties listed in the legislation, 61 passed it, 14 designated for tax bill freezes and 47 with the 5% cap; 12 counties rejected it; and 23 counties did not hold elections.
The law was challenged by two individuals, six school districts and one fire district. Forty-three counties, as well as individual county commissioners, later joined the case.
In his decision, Cole County Circuit Judge Christopher Limbaugh ruled that none of the plaintiffs had the right to sue and that they were wrong on the legal issues they raised.
Individuals do not have a right to sue simply because they believe they are at a disadvantage to a person in another county because of a property tax law, Limbaugh wrote. And the taxing districts can’t sue because they haven’t lost any money, he ruled.
The counties didn’t have the right to sue either, he wrote. They can’t raise issues on behalf of the school districts and other agencies they collect money for, he ruled.
“Missouri case law does not recognize standing based on dissatisfaction that other jurisdictions may impose different local taxes or conduct assessments differently; rather, Missouri case law recognizes standing where the plaintiff can show a present, direct adverse effect,” Limbaugh wrote.
The lawsuit was filed in September 2025, challenging the right of the legislature to write a law that provided property tax freezes in some counties, caps in others and no limits on increases in individual bills in 17 other counties and the city of St. Louis. The lawsuit alleged lawmakers used population and other characteristics to single out individual counties, creating special or local laws prohibited by the Missouri Constitution.
It was the second case challenging the stadium bill passed in a June 2025 special session. On Sept. 1, the Missouri Supreme Court heard an appeal in a separate lawsuit filed by two lawmakers and a conservative activist.
The court must decide whether state Sen. Mike Moon, an Ash Grove Republican, state Rep. Bryant Wolfin, a Ste. Genevieve Republican, and conservative activist Ron Calzone have standing. In January, Limbaugh ruled they did not and dismissed their lawsuit.
If the court finds Moon, Wolfin and Calzone do have standing, their case returns to Limbaugh.
The Missouri Supreme Court will also be asked to reverse Limbaugh in the case decided Wednesday, attorney Jim Layton said. Layton represents one of the individual plaintiffs and several other districts.

James’s marathon and carb-loading journeys actually predate his time as a celebrity. He raced his first marathon in Chicago in 2019, and has run a dozen since. On November 1, he’ll line up for his sixth consecutive New York City Marathon, but this time, he’s more focused on eating than on his time.

It’s a frigid Friday night in February in small-town Utah, and Conner Mantz and his wife, Kylie, are doing what they do pretty much every night: padding around in sweats, making pasta, talking. Usually about running. Lately, also about pregnancy, as Kylie is a few months in with their first—as are at least two of their neighbors. But tonight’s riveting topic? Home warranties.
Apparently, there is a crack in the ceiling of the couple’s new house. I don’t see it, but luckily, Kylie did, mere days before the one-year warranty on their four-bedroom, 4,500-square-foot new build in a master-planned community runs out.
I can’t help but notice, though: It looks like they just moved in. The kitchen as bare as a hotel kitchenette. A stack of cardboard boxes still unpacked. The bright-white interior is blank, save for a wooden sign propped on a table that reads “as for me and my house we will serve the Lord” (Joshua 24:15).
And an “art TV” presiding over the living room. The only reason I know it’s an art TV is because I have one, too. “The Frame,” by Samsung. A wall-mounted, bordered box designed to look like a painting or photograph, which you can choose from an extensive library, in lieu of the otherwise invasive screen it actually is. It was Conner’s Christmas gift to Kylie. Even though three years into their marriage, they have rarely, if ever, watched TV. “Which makes it kind of funny that we bought it!” says Kylie, scattering a bag of frozen broccoli florets onto a sheet pan. It’s also kind of funny, I think, that they have yet to select any art for the art TV, which renders it just an ordinary screen that’s seen neither Claude Monet nor the 2026 Winter Olympic Games, which at the time is well underway.
Maybe if it were the Summer Olympics?
Then again, if all goes according to his training plans, Conner won’t be tuning into the 2028 Games from his gray Costco couch in Mapleton, Utah. He’ll be running 26.2 miles through the streets of Los Angeles. Winning a medal. And breaking his personal record—which is the American marathon record: 2:04:43.
A record held for more than two decades by Khalid Khannouchi, until Conner declared last year that he would break it—and then, on a crisp October morning in Chicago, did. Only six seconds shy of third-place Kenya’s Alex Masai, knobby-kneed and nearly one minute faster than Khannouchi in London back in 2002, to a fourth-place—if otherwise undramatic—finish.

Why Goldman Sachs Still Calls Alphabet a Top AI Pick Despite the Earnings Miss
Alphabet shares cratered after snapping a 12-quarter earnings beat streak, yet one major Wall Street bank sees the selloff as a misreading of what actually drove the miss and where the real growth story is heading.
Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL | GOOGL Price Prediction) just ended a run of 12 straight quarterly earnings beats, and investors sold hard. Shares traded at $285.31 this morning, down 12.18% in the session. Business Insider reported that the drop erased a huge amount of market value. The miss looks worse than the business, though, and Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS) still rates the stock a Buy as a top AI pick.
An Investment Write-Down Drove the Miss
GAAP EPS came in at $2.12, missing the $2.97 consensus by 28.52%. Revenue of $127.58 billion was essentially in line with the $127.83 billion estimate and grew 24.6% year over year. An $8.7 billion loss on equity securities took $0.55 off EPS, so much of the shortfall came from an investment mark, with operations playing a smaller role. Operating income rose 29.93% to $40.58 billion.
Investment swings distort GAAP results across the group. During the quarter, Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) recorded a $207 million OpenAI gain, and Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) reported $53.4 billion of mostly Anthropic-related other income in its second quarter.
Search Growth Is the Key Question
Search and other revenue reached $63.35 billion, up 12%, which fell short of expectations. Goldman Sachs reports that management blamed currency headwinds and tougher comparisons, and described AI-driven searches as additive to the business rather than a drain on it. Chief Executive Sundar Pichai backed that up:
“Our AI investments are driving overall Search query growth, including commercial queries. In fact, our year-over-year query growth rate is the highest it’s been in the last five years.”
Cloud Is Growing Faster Than Azure and AWS
Google Cloud revenue grew 103%. Azure grew 48%, and AWS grew 37% in its most recent quarter. Pichai said:
“Google Cloud revenues grew 103%, powered by huge demand for our AI infrastructure and AI solutions. We’re also seeing strong demand for our TPU systems across a wide range of customers.”
Goldman Sachs reports that management cited a $561 billion backlog. Goldman Sachs says that figure is up 256%, and that management expects about 55% of it to turn into revenue within 24 months. Management also said compute availability is the main thing holding back even faster growth. Sundar Pichai said, “The Gemini app has reached one billion users.” Agents are the next product layer. These are Universal Cart and Gemini Agent in Search and Workspace, with plans to bring agents to Chrome and Android, all running on the Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon models.
Spending Opens a Free Cash Flow Gap
Capital spending reached $51.355 billion in the quarter, and free cash flow came in at negative $9.065 billion. Goldman Sachs reports that management repeated 2026 capex guidance of $195 billion to $205 billion and expects a further material increase in 2027. Goldman Sachs estimates about $203 billion for 2026 and about $350 billion for 2027. All of that spending has to be powered, cooled, and networked by someone, and we rounded up seven of those suppliers in a free AI infrastructure report. Salesforce has published merchant-side conversion numbers for agentic commerce product discovery, marking a shift from theoretical agentic potential to reported performance metrics. According to the Winter '27 Release, the company's Agentic Commerce Search capability is now delivering a 13% conversion lift and a 17% increase in add-to-cart rates. These figures, framed by the vendor as "early results," put a number on what agent-native discovery does to the funnel.
The Mechanic of Discovery
The underlying machinery driving these results relies on a dedicated small language model trained on each merchant's specific catalog and historical shopper behavior. By interpreting natural-language queries, the system surfaces products in real time, bypassing traditional keyword-based search filters. This approach is designed to move beyond static indexing, attempting to match the intent of a shopper's query directly to the inventory data provided by the merchant.
However, the efficacy of this model is tethered to the quality of the input. While the search capability is now standard for all Shopper Agent customers, the broader market readiness remains uneven. Our October 24 readiness analysis put the share of merchants holding the structured product data agents need at 15%. The search model trains on exactly that data. Without it, the performance gains Salesforce reports are not universally replicable across the enterprise landscape.
What the Numbers Leave Open

Missouri’s first report on the academic performance of students in its MOScholars voucher program found encouraging test scores but also exposed gaps in how the state collected the data, including information required by law that remains unavailable.
The report, released Wednesday by the Missouri Treasurer’s Office, found that students scored near the national average in reading and math during the program’s first three years. But researchers could validate test results for only 77% of students in testing grades, and the report lacked information about family income that state law requires.
The findings offer a baseline for measuring student performance but do not establish whether the program has improved academic outcomes or whether its students outperform those in public schools.
Researchers contracted to compile the report say they have an encouraging baseline to build on in future years. But the findings fall short of what some lawmakers expected from a program that has been operating for four years.
The law passed in 2021 that created the MOScholars program requires the state treasurer to “provide the test results and associated learning gains to the public via a state website after the third year of test and test-related data collection.”
Many expected this report last summer, immediately after the program’s third school year. Ahead of the Chicago Marathon, Clayton Young shared that he tore his hamstring, but still planned to compete. One of the strategies he said he used to get to the starting line and, ultimately, to the finish line as the first American: abandoning stretching in lieu of strength work—namely, isometric exercises.
When I heard this, I realized I had something in common with Young. My physical therapist, James Chung, PT, DPT, a sports performance physical therapist based in New York City, also recommends doing isometric strength exercises to deal with tendon issues, including my Achilles tendinopathy.
Isometrics are, indeed, great for pretty much everyone, says Mandy Fox, DPT, a physical therapist for runners in New York City. “An isometric exercise is a muscle contraction where the muscle produces force, but it doesn't change length and the joint angle doesn’t change,” Fox explains.
Basically, you’re loading the muscle and then holding it in one position for a set amount of time, like 30 seconds, as you would do in, say, a plank hold. This is in contrast to a concentric exercise, like lifting weights up to the top of a biceps curl, or an eccentric exercise, like slowly lowering heels down in a calf raise.
Whether you’re dealing with a hamstring tendon issue like Clayton, an Achilles tendon issue like me, or even a hip/glute tendon issue, this type of exercise can help. “This works because across the board, whether you’re elite or amateur, tendons respond to load, but they don’t respond to lengthening,” Fox says, adding that doing isometrics helps you keep running when you’re dealing with tendon issues.
While it’s always best to get evaluated by a doctor or physical therapist to rule out other factors that require a different approach, you can see a few common clues below that might point to a tendon-related injury and how isometrics can help.

For one, tendon pain is typically closer to where the joints are, says Chung, so you may feel Achilles tendon pain closer to the ankle and hamstring tendon issues at the sit bone or either side of the knee.
On the other hand, you’ll typically feel muscle strains or tears where the muscle contracts (and you feel pain when that happens). For example, with a calf strain, you might feel it most when you push off the ground, or with a hamstring strain, you might feel it most when your knee extends during the late swing phase of the gait cycle. You will also feel pain when you stretch a strained muscle.
Another way to tell: “Tendon pain is kind of dull and achy depending on what stage you’re in, but tendons will have what’s called a warmup effect where you’ll actually feel better when you warm it up,” Chung says, like after your first mile or two.

On Sunday, November 1, nearly 60,000 runners taking on the New York City Marathon will get the rare privilege of having city traffic stop for them as they cover 26.2 miles through the five boroughs. This year also marks 50 years since the race moved beyond its original Central Park loops in 1976, expanding into the citywide event we know today.
There's a lot to keep up with, from the professional races and returning champions to a surprisingly large number of celebrities attempting 26.2 miles. And with coverage stretching from early morning into Sunday night, you don't necessarily have to be standing along First Avenue or waiting near Central Park to catch everyone in action.
Here's what you need to know about watching the race, including start times, broadcasts, and how to follow individual runners.
What Time Does the 2026 NYC Marathon Start?
Things get going at 8 a.m. ET with the men's professional wheelchair division, followed by the women's wheelchair racers at 8:02 a.m. Handcycles and select athletes with disabilities start at 8:22 a.m., before the professional women take off at 8:35 a.m. and the men follow at 9:05 a.m.
The rest of the field will leave Staten Island in five waves, beginning at 9:10 a.m. and continuing through 11:30 a.m.
How to Watch the 2026 NYC Marathon
The main national broadcast starts at 8 a.m. ET on ESPN2, with coverage running until 11:30 a.m. If you'd rather stream, the ESPN app has the same coverage with an ESPN Unlimited plan, plus an extra hour of prerace programming beginning at 7 a.m. and more action through 1 p.m. There's a Spanish-language feed during the main 8 to 11:30 a.m. window as well.
In New York and the surrounding tri-state area, ABC7/WABC-TV is another option. Coverage begins at 7 a.m., ahead of the race broadcast from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m., which you can also stream on the ABC 7 New York app.
For anyone more interested in the finish line than the rest of the course, ABC7NY.com and the ABC 7 New York app have you covered from 10:30 a.m. until 6 p.m. with a dedicated live stream. That should give you plenty of time to catch the professionals and stick around for the thousands of other runners making their way into Central Park.
ABC also has a national Live from the TCS New York City Marathon special scheduled for 3 to 5 p.m. Later that evening, NYRR is giving the final finishers their own broadcast from 8 to 10 p.m. on ABC7NY.com and its YouTube channel. The celebrations don't have to end just because the fastest runners finished hours earlier.
How to Track Runners
Planning to cheer for someone in Brooklyn and then catch them again in Manhattan? Before hopping on the subway, you'll probably want to check how far along they are, which is where the official New York Road Runners app comes in handy.
You can track individual runners throughout the race, check their progress at timing points, and pull up leaderboards and results. The app is available for iOS and Android, and it also has live feeds for each of the four professional races if you want to keep an eye on the elites while you're out cheering.
Who to Watch at the 2026 NYC Marathon
Last year's champions, Benson Kipruto and Hellen Obiri, are both coming back, and each has a memorable performance to defend. Kipruto won the closest men's finish in NYC Marathon history in 2025, while Obiri ran 2:19:51 to break the women's course record that had stood for 22 years.
Conner Mantz and Zouhair Talbi are among the Americans to watch in the men's race.

The bronze bust of John Brown by Kansas sculptor Jim Brothers has the passion and movement of any Hellenistic masterpiece. Louis Copt’s painting of the Fox Creek Schoolhouse on the Kansas Tallgrass Prairie rivals the great Dutch master Johannes Vermeer’s “View of Delft.” The work of these fellow Midwesterners fires my imagination, inspires me, compels me to work harder, and pushes me to be a better teacher and writer.
Art is a catalyst in my life. It urges me from bed in the wee hours to plan a better way to convey some difficult concept to my students. It drives me to write, even when the words don’t come easily. Visual, literary, and musical art have pushed me to work and achieve my entire life. This has been especially true during the most trying times.
In the late ‘80s, fresh out of college, I started my first “real” job at an accounting firm, Laventhol & Horwath, in Philadelphia. Little did I know the firm was in dire straits. After eleven months I was laid off, and two months later the firm declared bankruptcy.
I was abruptly out of a job and unsure how I’d make rent. But I didn’t want friends or family to worry, so I kept my unemployment a secret.
In the morning, I dressed in a business suit like nothing was wrong and commuted to the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where I found solace. I absorbed the tranquility of the Japanese teahouse, and the sheer age of the medieval cloister put my short-term problems in perspective.
I sat with the work of great American painters. Among Thomas Eakins, Henry Ossawa Tanner, William Harnett, Charles Wilson Peale and others, I chose my next path. Their work renewed me, giving me the strength to carry on, the courage to decline opportunities in the corporate world, and the confidence to choose a more difficult road.
Soon I found a job at the University of Pennsylvania. My objective was to go back to school, and I knew the job provided tuition benefits. At Penn, once again, I found art to be my chief motivator. The fine arts library was designed in the nineteenth century by the great American architect Frank Furness. His masterpiece inspired me to keep going.
Every time the pressures of full-time work and graduate school made me want to drop out, I went to Furness’ library. I’d study in the main reading room for hours, and when fatigue set in, I needed only to look up at the vaulted ceiling, the strange American mix of Gothic and Romanesque influences, the terra-cotta, the leaded-glass windows ringed with maxims of encouragement and aphorisms like “Talkers are no great doers.”

Six years ago, when Joe Klecker was named to the inaugural class of the On Athletics Club (OAC) in Boulder, Colorado, his goals were all about racing fast on the track. But based on his physiology, his tenacity, and even his genes, coach Dathan Ritzenhein already knew Klecker was destined to become a marathoner—and probably a very good one.
When the team now known as OAC Global formed in the summer of 2020, it featured eight postcollegiate runners chasing Olympic berths from 1,500 to 10,000 meters. The OAC sent several runners (including Klecker) to the Tokyo Olympics and brought home medals from Paris.
But track success was only the first step of what Ritzenhein envisioned. In the years since, he and coach Laura Thweatt have built an elite marathon program, too.
Kenyan great Hellen Obiri, four-time Major Marathon winner and current women’s New York City Marathon course record holder, put OAC on the marathon map after joining in 2022. The progression of Klecker (with a marathon PR of 2:05:56 from Boston), along with newer teammates Ryan Ford (2:05:46 marathon PR) and Patrick Kiprop (59:14 half marathon PR), has helped to solidify the team’s presence on the roads.
As all four prepare for the NYC Marathon, we went behind the curtain at the OAC Global Training Facility in Boulder to learn what has fueled their success.
1. Play Off Other Runners’ Strengths in Training
When On recruited Obiri to Boulder in 2022, the two-time Olympic silver medalist at 5,000 meters was about to move up to the marathon. That meant shifting from pure track speed and relatively low mileage (80 miles per week) to 120- to 125-mile weeks and grinding sessions like 25K tempo runs.
With no other marathoners on the team, she did portions of her long runs with 10,000-meter runner Alicia Monson and some longer tempo efforts and fartleks with Klecker. All three benefited.
Obiri became one of the best marathoners in the world, winning New York and Boston twice and an Olympic bronze medal in Paris; Monson broke the American 5,000- and 10,000-meter records in 2023, and Klecker got a taste of what marathon training was all about, which gave him proper perspective as he was about to begin his first marathon build.

Google zero, eventually, comes for us all.
That's the belief, and fear, that meaningful traffic from Google trends toward zero because of changes to its search engine practices and, more recently, its shift toward AI — answering people's search questions not with links to places like websites, but with AI summaries and chatbot dialogue.
Reddit's (RDDT) latest earnings report was a reckoning of Google's AI-led changes. And it underscored how Silicon Valley's full embrace of AI may come at the cost of huge swaths of the web — and the companies that rely on Google traffic to operate.
"People still want Reddit. It is just Google is not sending them to Reddit the way they used to," Steve Huffman, Reddit's co-founder and CEO, said on an earnings call earlier this week.
The company reported that search referral traffic was down meaningfully in the past quarter. Google's shift to AI mode and AI overviews has halted traffic that once flowed to the social forum.
Reddit stock fell 30% on Friday.
"Google is crawling us as hard as ever, so the demand hasn't changed from their point of view either," Huffman said. "The reality is the AI Mode does not drive traffic. Not for us, and not to anybody as far as I know."
The shift toward a more AI-inflicted internet isn't just hurting Reddit. It's hurting Google too, at least in the short term. Its parent company, Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), shed almost $500 billion (or about two Netflixes) in market value after reporting a slowdown in its core search advertising business, in part due to the lower profitability of AI ads.
A critical view of the whole situation is that Google is smothering online publishers and sabotaging its own legacy business in its rush toward AI dominance.
But Reddit took a stance on the call that could be described as corporate Zen: "For AI Overviews and traffic, look, we don't control Google. We only control Reddit."
The company said it's not counting on that once-sweet Google traffic returning and plans to require all users to create Reddit accounts and sign in to access the site.
Other online publishers are looking to subscriptions to create direct relationships with audiences and are partnering with AI companies to ride the next wave of LLM-based media and product distribution.

The five biggest names in tech are now writing checks their operations alone cannot cover, and the gap between what they spend on AI and what they earn is widening fast enough to force choices that will hit shareholders directly.
Through the first nine months of 2026, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) together spent $556.9 billion on capital projects, mostly AI data centers. Their combined operating cash flow, which is the cash a business brings in from customers after paying its bills, reached a record $542.9 billion.
Capital spending had never topped operating cash flow in data going back to 2011. Free cash flow, meaning the cash left after capital spending, shifted to a $14 billion deficit from a $143.5 billion surplus a year earlier.

The five returned just 9.3% of operating cash flow as dividends and buybacks, down from 27.4%. That is the smallest share in at least 15 years.

This matters because buybacks shrink the share count, which lifts earnings per share even when profit stays flat. When buybacks stop and the company sells new shares, each share you own gets a smaller slice of the same profit.

Shipments fell 3% from a year earlier, and management said favorable weather had helped the prior-year quarter. After adjusting for the product mix, average selling prices rose 5%. Management said its adjusted EBITDA margin, a profit measure it uses, widened by 20 basis points to 32.3%.
Being the largest producer does not keep volumes from slipping. For example, Tesla still sells 54% of US electric cars, yet its deliveries slid from 1.81 million in 2023 to 1.64 million in 2025. Read Trefis Big Story: How Tesla Blundered.

My short answer to the question of what powered these stocks' surges is fear, not a sudden appreciation for dividends. Tech and AI-related stocks sold off hard in mid-October on worries about AI capital spending, and that money had to go somewhere. Consumer staples companies -- the boring, recession-resistant businesses that sell things people keep buying whether the economy is good or bad -- became the landing pad. The sector's valuation has climbed by enough that strategists now describe what's happening as a defensive rotation rather than a sign of stronger demand.
Beyond that broader shift in market sentiment, both companies gave investors real reasons to show up: On Oct. 22, P&G delivered fiscal first-quarter results that beat estimates, with organic sales growth accelerating to 4%, driven for once by actual volume growth rather than just price increases. The stock jumped roughly 6% that day, its biggest single-day move since early 2020.
On Tuesday, Coca-Cola delivered a Q3 report that helped justify its prior run-up -- it beat estimates on both the top and bottom lines (revenue rose 7% to $13.4 billion, non-GAAP EPS rose 11% to $0.91). What these companies are doing shows they are still active. This month alone, P&G closed its $3.9 billion acquisition of supplement brand Thorne, expanding its footprint in the premium wellness niche. Coca-Cola, for its part, just announced that in 2027, it will pick up KFC's U.S. beverage business, ending PepsiCo's roughly 40-year run as the fried chicken chain's supplier.

Here's my take: Neither of these stocks' recent upsurges tells you much about whether they will be good investments for the next five years. Investors' recent rotation out of AI stocks and into consumer staples came in reaction to short-term fears, so it shouldn't be viewed as a verdict on the long-term business outlook for Coca-Cola or Procter & Gamble. If the market's worries over AI capex fade next month, some of this money could rotate right back into tech, and these stocks could easily give back some of their gains.
Jumping into a stock because it just had a good month is the same mistake as avoiding a stock because it just had a bad one -- you're reacting to a few weeks of price action instead of judging the actual business and what you're paying for it. The things that matter here are whether the businesses' underlying growth drivers (P&G's returning volume, Coke's raised guidance) are real and durable. "Buy tech bond 'diamonds-in-rough' as AI hyperscalers up equity issuance, cut buybacks," Michael Hartnett, chief investment strategist at Bank of America, said in his latest Flow Show note.
The call comes after a punishing year for tech credit.
Why Hartnett Calls Tech Bonds 'Diamonds in the Rough'
According to Hartnett, U.S. technology bonds have lost about 9% so far in 2026.
That leaves their total return relative to the broad investment-grade bond index at the lowest level in 30 years. In other words, tech debt has rarely looked this cheap compared with the rest of the high-grade market.
